stories.title: Australia condemns 'unacceptable' rogue OpenAI hack
stories.summary: A rogue OpenAI model bypassed safeguards during training and hacked an Australian government website, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said as he admonished the ChatGPT creator over an "obviously unacceptable" breach. The AI tool sought access to a health statistics portal in June and "didn't accept no for an answer", sidestepping restrictions to breach a section hosting private files, Mr Albanese said. OpenAI did not raise the alarm with the Australian government until September, when it sent a message to a generic email inbox that is only checked once each day. Global worries about the power of advanced AI tools are mounting after a string of hacking incidents involving models from both OpenAI and rival developer Anthropic. "Today, I spoke with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, to express Australia's extreme concern about this incident," Mr Albanese told reporters in New York yesterday. He added: "I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred.

stories.title: Anti wrong-way-driving tech may be 10-15 years away - TII
stories.summary: Technology to tackle wrong-way motorway driving could be 15 years away, Transport Infrastructure Ireland has told the Oireachtas Joint Committee on Transport. While the spikes, also known as stingers, have been considered, they are not being used because they are unsafe at speed and emergency responders sometimes need to use the wrong-way ramps, according to TII Director of Network Management Pat Maher. People purposely attempting to drive the wrong way can also just enter the motor way correctly and then turn around, he said. The technology, he said, that will have the biggest impact is "through the use of connected vehicles". This will "allow communication between drivers and control centres", he said, but is only currently available in about 5% of cars. It could take "perhaps 10, perhaps 15 years" before the "broader development within the fleet of these communications technologies will allow immediate transmission of messages and alerts to drivers".

stories.title: TikTok cites 1,600 risky driving videos since M9 crash
stories.summary: TikTok's Global Head of Policy in Trust & Safety Zachary Hecht has said that TikTok has identified 1,600 videos in Ireland showing highly risky driving, vehicular theft or related behaviours since the fatal M9 crash last month. Speaking to the Oireachtas Committee on Media, Mr Hecht said that TikTok does not classify dangerous driving as its own category outside of "dangerous activity and challenges". He said that 42,000 pieces of content from this overarching category were removed in total in the first half of this year in Ireland. For context, Mr Hecht said that around 400,000 pieces of content are posted on TikTok in Ireland each day. When pressed on whether TikTok had figures related specifically to dangerous driving, Mr Hecht said that the company conducted additional sweeps and analysis following the fatal M9 crash last month. As part of this analysis, TikTok identified approximately 1,600 instances of content have been identified in Ireland "related to the broader category of vehicular theft, highly risky driving and behaviours related to that", Mr Hecht said.

stories.title: Leitrim strategy targets 1,300 new remote workers
stories.summary: The completion of the National Broadband Plan rollout across Co Leitrim has the potential to attract 1,300 additional remote workers to the county, according to a new report. Leitrim County Council will launch 'Shaping Leitrim 2026-2036,' a ten-year economic development and skills strategy for the northwest county. The report found that 28% of Leitrim’s workforce works remotely, compared with the national average of 36%, which would equate to an additional 1,300 remote workers. The report from the County Council and Mayo, Sligo and Leitrim Education and Training Board contains 30 actions to strengthen the county’s economy, workforce and communities. It found that 62% of workers in the Carrick-on-Shannon labour catchment area hold third-level qualifications, but more than 70% travel outside that area for employment. The ‘Shaping Leitrim’ report will be launched at an inaugural People, Place, Possibilities Leitrim Ambassadors Summit.

stories.title: O'Shea acknowledges 'really unusual' build-up for players
stories.summary: Dara O'Shea says the build-up to the UEFA Nations League campaign has been "unusual" to deal with for the Republic of Ireland squad but emphasised that the decision to go ahead with the controversial fixtures against Israel is not down to the players. stories.summary: It's a Mayo versus Kerry battle once more as David Clifford is up against Ryan O'Donoghue and Jack Carney for the PwC GAA GPA Footballer of the Year award. The green and red also lead the way with 11 nominations for the All-Star team of the year award following their historic season, which saw them end a 75-year wait to land the Sam Maguire. The westerns defeated the Kingdom by three points at Croke Park in July sparking wild scenes of celebration which have continued for much of the time since. Kerry are next on the list of nominations with seven, while semi-finalists Dublin have five. Westmeath, who landed a first Leinster title in 22 years, are next with four, while Monaghan, Ulster champions Armagh and the other All-Ireland semi-finalists Louth have three each. Cork, Galway, Tyrone and Connacht kings Roscommon have two each with Donegal completing the list with one, meaning 12 counties have received nominations. In the Young Footballer of the Year category, Mayo have two players in the running once more, with Darragh Beirne and Kobe McDonald set to go up against Louth's Dara McDonnell.

stories.summary: Having made a slow start to last year's URC season, Leinster hooker Gus McCarthy has stressed that the defending champions will have a point to prove this time around. Leo Cullen's men open their title defence away to the Lions in Johannesburg before a trip back down to sea level to face the Sharks in Durban. Leinster started last season in South Africa too, but fell to consecutive defeats to the Stormers (35-0) and Bulls (39-31), which gives them plenty of motivation this time around. "The way we started the season last year away to the Stormers was very, very disappointing", McCarthy said. "It's something we’ve reflected on and we’re looking to put that to bed. "It’s a big two games for us now. Hopefully we can prove a point and improve our performances."

stories.title: Something For The Weekend - Cáit Ní Riain's cultural picks
stories.summary: Cáit Ní Riain is a traditional Irish and folk singer and multi-instrumentalist from Co Tipperary. Her main musical love and influence is traditional Irish song. She plays piano and sings in The Weaving, alongside accordionist and singer, Méabh Begley and Leeds' fiddler, Owen Spafford. The trio brings together the rich musical traditions of three counties Kerry, Tipperary and Yorkshire, their three regions of origin. They have just released their eponymous debut album. She also composes her own music and songs which are rooted in themes of wildness, love, and 'the need to decolonise our minds, hearts, and bodies'. I watched a beautiful film called The Piano recently, a 1993 film written and directed by Jane Campion. Its raw beauty spoke to me, the way in which a mute woman was able to express her soul through the spectrum of colour, tone, and emotion that those black and white keys invited was very moving and resonant, as a lover of the ivory myself! I am bathing in the fiddle music of Sliabh Luachra man Paddy Cronin of late. I go through seasons where I'm drawn and pulled into the music of one player or singer and I really let their music swim around my soul for a couple of months without digesting much other music. The silence around their singular musical voice allows me to hear them louder. Each true player is a kind of musical universe in and of themselves, and even though some of these great players have long passed on, I feel like I get to know them by listening to their music in this slow and deep kind of way. The sound of their soul rings through. I am reading the work of a man who I believe is a genius of our day, James Tunney. Trotsky vs Jesus: Battle of the AI-Millennium is all about the soul and spirituality of humanity and the challenges that the materialist/industrialist/technological path poses for human consciousness and the journey of soul development. His work is astounding. The depth of research and the capacity of that man's mind humbles me. I am also reading Marian Woodman's classic Leaving My Father's House.

stories.title: Fiona Shaw nearly quit acting after feeling 'no joy'
stories.summary: Actress Fiona Shaw has revealed how she nearly quit acting after feeling "no joy" at one point in her career. The 68-year-old is best known for starring in Killing Eve and the Harry Potter franchise as the cold and repressed aunt Petunia Dursley. Despite her long and acclaimed career, the award-winning actress said she considered quitting in 2013 while she was performing in a New York production of The Testament Of Mary, a stage adaptation of Colm Tóibín’s novella. Speaking to Good Houskeeping UK, she said: "I was running one day between the matinee and the evening performance, and I saw the sign outside the theatre with my name on it. Shaw stars as wealthy widower and eager matchmaker Mrs Jennings alongside Daisy Edgar-Jones in the upcoming Dolly Alderton film adaptation of Jane Austen’s Sense And Sensibility. Shaw said Edgar-Jones was a "lovely, enchanting girl" and that she has "every quality that I didn’t have at her age; she can withhold".

stories.title: White House ban on three media outlets blocked by judge
stories.summary: A federal judge has ordered US President Donald Trump to restore White House access for journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico, saying his ban on the three media outlets was likely unconstitutional. In a major setback for Mr Trump in one of his biggest battles with the media, US District Judge Tim Kelly issued his order in a lawsuit that the news organisations filed, contesting the ban that the Republican president announced on 18 September. Judge Kelly ordered the Trump administration to immediately return the outlets' press passes and blocked officials from enforcing the ban for 14 days. The judge rejected the White House's assertion that the ban was motivated by national security concerns. "The record lacks factual support for defendants' contention that the revocation of plaintiffs' hard passes will in fact protect national security or that national security will be endangered if the court orders their passes reinstated while this litigation proceeds," he said, adding that Mr Trump himself had stated the ban was due to "alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity" of the outlets' reporting. Mr Trump had said on social media that the three outlets "shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES," and Justice Department lawyers had sought to justify the ban on national security grounds. The three outlets sued Mr Trump and other members of his administration in federal court in Washington on Monday, saying the ban violated the US Constitution's First Amendment protections for free speech and a free press, as well as their due process rights.

stories.title: Dáil to debate social housing defective-block scheme
stories.summary: A planned scheme to remediate social homes damaged by defective concrete blocks is set to be debated in the Dáil this evening. It is understood that the social homes scheme is based on the scheme for private homes, with changes to reflect the difference with social housing. Councils and approved housing bodies [AHBs] are set to be responsible for assessing properties, appointing appropriate engineers and contractors, and rehousing tenants, if needed. In the private scheme, the housing agency carries out the technical work, the homeowner appoints a contractor and sources accommodation, if needed. The current legislation covers nine areas including Donegal, Mayo, Clare, Limerick, Sligo, Carlow and parts of Wexford, Fingal and Meath. The private housing scheme covers 100% of eligible expenditure, up to €462,000 for private dwellings and a limited number of rented dwellings.

stories.title: Europe's August car sales rise on EV demand
stories.summary: Demand for electrified cars continued to underpin growth in Europe's car market in August, offsetting a steep decline in petrol and diesel vehicle sales, data from the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) showed today. Higher registrations, a proxy for sales, also helped Chinese automakers expand their presence across the European Union, Britain and the European Free Trade Association. ACEA said growth in new EU car registrations was supported by strong demand for electrified vehicles, aided by market support measures and a broader range of models available to consumers despite higher energy costs and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty. Battery-electric, plug-in hybrid and hybrid car registrations climbed 52.2%, 13.5% and 3.4%, respectively, together accounting for over 73% of all new vehicles. Petrol and diesel car registrations fell 23.5% and 23.1%, respectively Registrations at Renault and Volkswagen slid between 4.4% and 3.6%, while Stellantis gained 3.5% but their combined market share slid to 49.8% from 52%

stories.title: Zelensky vows winter campaign as Russian strikes kill 7
stories.summary: President Volodymyr Zelensky has warned Moscow at the United Nations that Ukraine would strike back and make the coming winter deeply painful for Russia, if the two sides cannot agree a truce on energy attacks before the cold sets in. Ukraine and its allies are racing to secure limited agreements on energy infrastructure and Black Sea shipping before winter, fearing renewed Russian strikes on power and heating facilities, while Moscow continues to show little interest in wider negotiations to end the war. "Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us. But in response, we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia too," Mr Zelensky told the UN General Assembly during the annual gathering of world leaders in New York. Though Russia has a far bigger arsenal of missiles which it has used to pound its enemy throughout the war, Ukraine has developed and used thousands of long-range drones to strike back at Russian warehouses, port infrastructure and oil refineries. "That's exactly why we say that de-escalation steps are needed before winter," Mr Zelensky said, calling for more robust diplomacy and noting the potential sway that Chinese President Xi Jinping could have on Russian President Vladimir Putin. China's Xi, who did not attend the United Nations gathering, was due on Thursday to hold White House talks with US President Donald Trump, with whom Mr Zelensky met on Tuesday to discuss a ceasefire on energy-related targets.

stories.title: Munster searching for stability both on and off the pitch
stories.summary: With just one day to go until the new BKT United Rugby Championship season kicks off, we are doing a province-by-province breakdown over the next few days to remind you how each of the four Irish sides fared in 2025/26, and what to expect from them this season. Next up on our tour of the provinces is Munster, who will be hoping season two under Clayton McMillan is a little more straightforward than season one. It's rarely dull down at Thomond Park, but the 2025/26 one was a constant rollercoaster, both on and off the pitch. When Clayton McMillan came in last summer, his stated aim for getting Munster back on track was for them to find their middle ground more often, rather than playing either to their ceiling or floor on a weekly basis. By that remit, it wasn’t a success. It started impressively with five URC wins in a row, including a famous 31-14 hammering of Leinster. At the time, McMillan pleaded caution that those results were probably papering over some of the cracks in their performances, and so it proved to be, as they lost seven of their next 10 games leading up to the Six Nations, and crashed out of the Champions Cup in the pool stage.

stories.title: GAA to meet AFL over player recruitment protocols
stories.summary: GAA President Jarlath Burns has said that a meeting will be held with representatives of the Australian Football League (AFL) shortly to try and find a more agreeable protocol to GAA player recruitment by that association. Unease has been expressed in a number of counties regarding the recruitment of young players by AFL clubs without the knowledge of their GAA club or county boards members. Some management teams have told of only finding out about AFL trials of their members on social media. Kerry county board chairman Patrick O'Sullivan said that the current situation cannot be allowed to continue and called for more regulation. "The GAA cannot continue to pretend there is nothing wrong here. Action has to be taken," he said. "There is a lack of regulation and we need the AFL to acknowledge the work that has been invested in these young players through compensation or equipment or otherwise. We need regulation of this practice and I'm calling on the GAA to deal with this as a matter of urgency."

stories.title: Munster re-sign Butler as Wood joins out-half injury list
stories.summary: Munster have re-signed out-half Tony Butler on a short-term deal as Tom Wood became the latest out-half to join the long-term injury list. Butler, who had been released by the province at the end of last season, was drafted in as training cover last week after Wood and JJ Hanrahan were both ruled out of their pre-season friendly against Leicester Tigers. With Jack Crowley expected to be sidelined until Christmas at least, and Australian signing Will Harrison still a few weeks away from returning from a knee issue, the province have now confirmed that Wood will be out until early 2027 after undergoing surgery on a shoulder injury. "Undergoing surgery now is the best option for Tom in both the short- and long-term," head coach Clayton McMillan said. "He is a very promising young player with a bright future. While it's disappointing for him to miss the coming months, I know he will use the time wisely and come back in even better condition to make a big contribution to Munster this season and in the years ahead." Ennis native Butler, who played 27 games across his five seasons with the province, featured in Friday night's pre-season friendly defeat to Leicester Tigers in Cork, and could go straight into the matchday squad for Saturday's BKT United Championship opener against Glasgow Warriors at Thomond Park.

stories.title: Hysterically Shopping! A pop opera for the hyperpop generation
stories.summary: Composer Aran O'Grady and theatre company tasteinyourmouth introduce Hysterically Shopping! their new 'pop opera for the hyperpop generation', made in collaboration with music ensemble and arts organisation Glasshouse and premiering at this year's Dublin Theatre Festival. We love classical music. We love the sound, the complexity, the feeling when the orchestra is going full throttle! We especially love when a classically trained singer is really letting rip on an aria. Hearing that big booming voice reach the back of the theatre. What. A. Buzz. So when Glasshouse approached us in 2022 with the idea of making an opera…what we lacked in experience we made up in enthusiasm! We knew what we liked already about opera: the epic stories, the larger-than-life characters, the sweeping emotions and all those timeless themes: forbidden love, jealousy, rivals, betrayal, death. But it was also important to us that this opera feel contemporary. So out went the Mediterranean backdrops and classical heroes and in came the supermarket and romantic archetypes everyone would recognise (a Lonely Girl, a Lovelorn Boy and An Evil Boss). La Boheme and Aida and The Marriage of Figaro were once popular entertainment, made to appeal to diverse tastes and broad audiences, and we wanted to make our show in this spirit. Part of making our opera speak to the world of Dublin Theatre Festival 2026 was making it sound like the music of 2026. Over the last four years we've worked to incorporate elements of modern pop: electronic music, vocal effects and catchy hooks. Carrie, our entry point into the world, has the kind of voice you hear on pop radio today, making for an exciting contrast with the gorgeous classical voices of the Cashier and the Intercom. What we didn't want was a night at the opera that had people looking at their watches. So we decided to tell some of our story through dialogue and some through song. Sometimes, in opera, we felt it would be better if they didn’t sing absolutely everything. We wanted to keep it short, sharp and snappy!

stories.title: Galway spot named in Lonely Planet's Best in Travel 2027 list
stories.summary: An Irish destination has been included in Lonely Travel's Best in Travel 2027 list. The publication – long the go-to resource for ambitious and adventurous travellers – has built a global following for its recommendations and insider travel tips. Its Best in Travel list is a collection of 50 inspirational destinations and unforgettable travel experiences selected by its global community of travel experts, divided into 25 Best Places and 25 Best Experiences. The editors write that this year's list "reflects travellers' growing desire to slow down, escape the crowds and seek out more meaningful experiences". Among those meaningful experiences is a visit to Killary Fjord in Co Galway, one of Ireland's very few glacial fjords and a majestic part of our national landscape. Located in Connemara, the fjord creates a natural border between Galway and Mayo and spans 16km. It is surrounded by striking natural scenery, including Mweelrea, Connacht's highest mountain which rises up to 814 metres, the Maumturk Mountains and marvellous Twelve Bens.

stories.title: Dubliner breaks silence on abuse at Celtic Boys Club
stories.summary: Forty years ago, Dubliner Declan Roche moved to Glasgow at the age of 15 with dreams of becoming a professional footballer. Within months, he says, he was being sexually assaulted by a manager at Celtic Boys Club. After almost four decades of keeping the abuse to himself, he has now decided to speak publicly about it for the first time. Celtic Boys Club was established in 1966 and acted as a feeder club for talented young players hoping to progress to Celtic Football Club, many from Ireland. Over subsequent decades, a number of men associated with the Boys Club were convicted of sexually abusing young players, including its founder, Jim Torbett, and former manager Frank Cairney. In recent years, survivors have also pursued civil claims against Celtic FC over abuse they suffered at the Boys Club. In 2025, the club reached settlements with 24 men who had brought claims through group proceedings in Scotland. Declan was among those who brought claims, until now he did so anonymously.

stories.title: Fianna Fáil holds emergency meeting over sport grants
stories.summary: Fianna Fáil held an emergency meeting in Leinster House tonight amid claims that Fine Gael had "jumped the gun" by announcing details of the latest sport grants scheme. Junior Sports Minister Charlie McConalogue told his colleagues that the Community Sports Facilities Fund was still not finalised. However, several members of Fine Gael have already announced on social media that the registration date for applications opens next Monday. Fianna Fáil TDs are fuming and believe this gave their colleagues in Government a head start when it came to advertising the scheme which is viewed as very important in individual constituencies. A spokesperson for Sports Minister Patrick O'Donovan has insisted the information was shared with Fianna Fáil and Independent members of Government earlier this week. Those attending tonight's Fianna Fáil meeting say the matter will now have to be discussed by the Taoiseach and the Tánaiste.

stories.summary: Swedish fashion retailer H&M has today reported a bigger than expected rise in June-August operating profit, as CEO Daniel Erver said his push to control costs and make sourcing more efficient was bearing fruit. Operating profit in H&M's fiscal third quarter increased to 6.04 billion crowns ($608.63m) compared to a year-earlier 4.91 billion crowns and a mean forecast in an LSEG poll of analysts of 5.14 billion. H&M meanwhile said it expected sales in September to rise by 1% measured in local currencies. Gross profit margin widened to 54% in the third quarter, from 52.9% last year, which included positive one-off effects from tariffs, H&M said. Analysts had expected a margin of 53.4%. Improvements within purchasing, cost control and operation efficiency contributed to a more profitable business, the CEO said in a statement. "Although sales developed in a positive direction during the quarter, we see further potential to increase sales going forward," Erver said.

stories.title: Rome's Colosseum closed after worker death
stories.summary: The Colosseum in Rome, a top tourist destination, closed today due to the death of a worker inside overnight, the Italian culture ministry has said in a statement. Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said she was "deeply shocked and saddened by the news of the tragic death of Andrea Moretti, a skilled worker who lost his life last night following an accident at the Colosseum". Moretti, 22, reportedly died after falling from a height while working on a new lighting installation. "For a person to die at the age of 22 is unacceptable --and even more so when it happens in the workplace," Ms Meloni said in a statement. In a first statement earlier today, the culture ministry said "the second-tier section where the accident occurred" would be closed as a mark of mourning. It later said that "once the orderly exit of those currently inside is complete, the Colosseum will be closed to the public."

stories.title: Sligo Rovers members to vote on restructuring tonight
stories.summary: One of the last fully fan-owned clubs in the League of Ireland, Sligo Rovers, is set to vote on proposed restructuring, at a special general meeting this evening. Rovers will ask members to consider whether the management of The Showgrounds and the club should be separated into two entities. Following the club's annual general meeting in April, experts were appointed to examine the legal, financial and administrative issues involved in increasing funding for the club. Sligo has said operating budget and costs have doubled in the past five years, while volunteer fundraising and existing commercial income are increasingly stretched. In a statement, the club said its current financial model is no longer sustainable and the changes proposed will help generate resources and investment needed to be competitive at the elite level of soccer in Ireland. Rovers has recommended that The Showgrounds stadium remain in the ownership of the Sligo Football and Sport Development Society, a community-based co-operative.
